title: Content with right action
hook: the mind is content with itself when it acts rightly (Meditations 7.28)

segments.voice: Yesterday: Marcus on thinking of what you have, and how you'd miss it. Your line was what I have. What did you name when you caught yourself wanting? Day five hundred ninety-two.

You return a wallet you found on the sidewalk. Nobody's watching. There's no reward, no thank-you note, no story to tell at dinner, and the owner never even learns your name. And yet you walk away a little lighter. Something in you settles, like a picture hanging straight. Where does that feeling come from, when nothing outside you changed? Marcus Aurelius had an answer, and it's one of the shortest entries in book seven.

First, the instruction. Meditations seven, twenty-eight, begins, in George Long's translation: "Retire into thyself." Go inward. Not to hide, but to check what's there. Second, what you find. Marcus says the ruling part of the mind, what the Stoics called the hegemonikon, has a particular nature. It's content with itself when it does what's just, and that brings it calm. That's the whole entry. Notice what's missing. No applause. No result. The mind's contentment doesn't depend on whether the wallet's owner is grateful, or whether anyone knows. It comes from the act itself. Third, why that matters. If your peace depends on outcomes, you're always waiting. Waiting for thanks, for the plan to work, for people to notice. Marcus is pointing at a source of satisfaction that's fully in your control. You can't make the world reward you. You can do the right thing, and the mind, he says, is built to be content with that. Fourth, a fair caution. Some people hear this as smugness: being pleased with yourself for being good. That's not quite it. Marcus elsewhere warns against wanting credit even from yourself, comparing the good person to a vine that bears grapes and asks for nothing. The contentment here is quieter. Less a pat on the back, more the click of a key turning in the right lock. You did the fitting thing, and the mind settles, the way a picture hangs straight.
screen: `RETIRE INTO YOURSELF.` · `THE RULING MIND IS CONTENT.` · `PEACE NOT WAITING ON OUTCOMES.` · `NOT SMUG: A KEY IN A LOCK.` · then, large: `CONTENT WITH RIGHT.`

segments.voice: Sit, and breathe. Remember one right thing you did recently that nobody noticed. Washing a dish that wasn't yours. Telling the truth when a lie was easier. Being patient on the phone. Let the memory settle. Notice if there's a quiet rightness in it, a straightness. Don't inflate it. Don't dismiss it. Just let yourself enjoy it, the way you'd enjoy warm sun. Rest there. The bell holds the time.
Vine. Marcus's image for the good person: a vine that bears grapes and asks for nothing. Today's word.
Your line: content with right. Today, do one right thing that no one will notice, and let yourself enjoy it quietly, without telling anyone. Day five hundred ninety-two.

howItsDone: Readers of Marcus often notice the quiet satisfaction of doing something right that nobody sees, and treat it as enough, rather than waiting for thanks or results.

myth: Marcus says the ruling mind is content when it acts justly
and that this brings it calm, whatever the outcome.
Marcus says the contentment comes from being praised
it comes from the act itself; praise isn't part of it.

fork.setup: you did the right thing, and nobody thanked you or even noticed. by 7.28, what's left?
options: the mind's own contentment in having acted rightly.
fork.reveal: Meditations 7.28: the ruling principle is content with itself when it does what is just, and so finds calm.

original.note: Greek: the ruling part, the Stoic word for the mind's command center, which Marcus refers to in 7.28.

trapdoor: what you thought: be proud of yourself for being good.
what it means: doing what's just brings its own quiet calm, with no need for applause, even your own.
what a scholar hears: hegemonikon is the Stoic term for the soul's ruling faculty, seated in the heart in early Stoic theory, which assents to impressions and chooses actions.
recall: no stepping in the same river twice
a sea gone flat after wind

notes: Confirm Long's 'Retire into thyself.' as the opening of 7.28, and the paraphrase of the rest (the ruling principle content with itself when it does what is just, and so secures tranquility).
Confirm that the Greek of 7.28 refers to the hegemonikon (to logikon hegemonikon).
The vine bearing grapes without seeking credit is 5.6; confirm.
Early Stoics (Chrysippus) located the hegemonikon in the heart; confirm phrasing in the trapdoor.
